Where is Portland and what does its layout mean for a house sale?

Portland sits where the Willamette and Columbia rivers meet, in Multnomah County, with small pieces of the city reaching into Clackamas and Washington counties. The city covers about 145 square miles, and the Willamette runs north through downtown and splits it into east and west halves.

Addresses are organized into six sectors: North, Northeast, Northwest, Southeast, Southwest and South. Burnside Street separates north from south. A house in Northeast near Alberta or Hollywood, one in Southeast near Hawthorne or Belmont, and one in St. Johns in the North sector can sit only a few miles apart and still draw very different buyers and repair needs.

The ground matters too. Portland is built over the Boring Lava Field, and a 2014 report flagged more than 7,000 locations at high risk for landslides and soil liquefaction in a major earthquake. Council Crest rises to 1,073 feet on the west side, while Mount Tabor, at 636 feet, is the high point east of the river. A hillside lot in the west hills and a flat lot in the east carry different foundation, drainage and insurance questions.

What do Portland's weather and soil do to an older house?

Portland has cool, wet winters and warm, dry summers, so moisture is the main wear factor on a house here. Measurable precipitation falls on about 157 days a year, and annual rainfall runs about 36.9 inches at the airport and 44.1 inches downtown.

Snow is light, about 4 inches a year, so roofs rarely fail from snow load. Long wet seasons are harder on roofing, gutters, siding and crawlspaces, and those are the items a buyer's inspector looks at closely.

Heat is part of the picture as well. The city's record high is 116 degrees, set on June 28, 2021, and about 61 days a year reach 80 degrees or higher.

  • Record low: minus 3 degrees, on February 2, 1950
  • Typical December daytime high: 46.9 degrees
  • Annual sunshine: about 2,341 hours
  • USDA hardiness zone: 8b, with parts of downtown in 9a

Who employs people in Portland, and why does it affect sellers?

Portland's job base leans on health care, technology, athletic apparel and shipping, and those employers shape which neighborhoods draw buyers. Total nonfarm employment in the city was 440,797 in 2024, and education and health services was the largest sector at 116,498 jobs.

The city's biggest employers by headcount include the following.

The Port of Portland handles more than 13 million tons of cargo a year and ranks third on the West Coast for export tonnage. A seller whose house is near a hospital campus, a rail stop or the river industrial areas often fields different questions from buyers than a seller in a quiet residential pocket.

How do I get around Portland, and does transit help a sale?

TriMet runs the region's buses and MAX light rail, and the Portland Streetcar is a separate city-owned system that TriMet operates under contract.

MAX has five lines, Blue, Green, Orange, Red and Yellow, covering about 60 miles with 96 stations. The first line opened in 1986 between Portland and Gresham. The Red Line reaches Portland International Airport, and TriMet carried about 66 million riders in 2025.

Bridges also shape daily travel. Downtown spans over the Willamette include Hawthorne (1910), Steel (1912), Broadway (1913), Burnside (1926), Ross Island (1926), Marquam (1966) and Tilikum Crossing (2015).

What is the Home Energy Score, and does my Portland house need one?

Most Portland houses that are publicly advertised for sale need a Home Energy Score and report before the listing goes up. The score has to appear in every ad, including the RMLS, online listings, yard signs and print, and the seller is ultimately responsible for compliance.

Sellers who sell privately with no public advertising are not covered. Other points from the city's guidance:

  • The rule follows the City of Portland boundary, not the mailing address. Some Portland addresses sit outside the city.
  • An existing score and report can be reused for up to eight years if the home has not changed.
  • Manufactured, mobile and floating homes cannot be scored and are not required to have one.
  • Sellers in certain financial distress, or with a condemned or uninhabitable house, may apply for an exemption.
  • Income-qualified sellers at or below 80 percent of Portland's area median income may be able to get a free score through Community Energy Project.

A sale that is not publicly advertised avoids the score step entirely, which matters to owners who would rather skip a pre-listing assessment. You can read the full rule on the City of Portland Home Energy Score page.

What happens if my Portland house has a tenant in it?

A Portland landlord who ends a tenancy without cause, or chooses not to renew a fixed term, generally owes the tenant relocation assistance. The city sets the amounts by unit size.

Written notice has to go out at least 90 days ahead and must state the amount the tenant is eligible for. A landlord who skips the process can owe up to three times the monthly rent plus actual damages and attorney fees. One listed exemption covers a fixed-term tenancy where the tenant was told in advance that the home would be sold or permanently converted, and most exemptions need a filing with the Portland Housing Bureau.

These costs are one reason owners of occupied rentals look at a cash sale where the tenant stays in place or the timing is agreed up front. The Portland Housing Bureau page and its helpdesk at 503-823-1303 can confirm how the rules apply to your lease.

When are Multnomah County property taxes due on a Portland home?

Multnomah County bills Portland homes in three installments, due November 16, February 16 and May 17 for the 2026 tax year. Paying in full earns a 3 percent discount, and paying two-thirds earns 2 percent. A payment must be received or postmarked by the due date to keep the discount and avoid interest.

The county's Division of Assessment, Recording and Taxation sends the statements. A green statement means the owner pays directly, and a yellow one means a mortgage company may pay on the owner's behalf. Real market value for 2026 is set as of January 1, 2026, and the appeal deadline is December 31, 2026.

Oregon's Measures 5 and 50 tie taxes to an assessed value that generally cannot rise more than about 3 percent a year, even when the market value climbs faster. A long-held Portland house often has an assessed value well below its market value, so the tax bill a buyer sees on the old owner's statement can change after a sale reset. The county statement guide explains each part of the bill.

What must a seller disclose on an Oregon house, and how does that play out in Portland?

Oregon requires most sellers of residential property to give each buyer who makes a written offer a seller's property disclosure statement. The form covers title, water, sewage, insulation, structure, systems, seismic and general conditions, and the buyer has five days after delivery to revoke unless the buyer waives that right.

Some sellers use a limited exclusion and complete only Section 1 of the form. Listed exclusions include a first sale of a never-occupied dwelling, sales by a financial institution after foreclosure, sales by a court-appointed personal representative, trustee, conservator or guardian, and sales by a government agency. The statute is ORS 105.464 and 105.470.

In Portland, seismic and slope questions on that form carry real weight given the landslide and liquefaction mapping. An inherited house sold by an estate representative may qualify for the shorter form, which is one reason families handling a probate property ask about a direct sale.

What choices does a Portland seller have?

A Portland owner can list with an agent, sell without one, or sell to a cash buyer. Each path trades time, cost and certainty differently.

  • Listing: usually needs a Home Energy Score, photos, showings and a repair negotiation after inspection.
  • Selling without an agent: saves the listing-side commission but puts marketing and paperwork on you.
  • Cash sale: sold as-is, with a closing date the seller helps choose.

Yes, if you publicly advertise the home for sale inside the City of Portland, with a few exceptions such as manufactured homes. A private sale with no public advertising is not covered. A report can be reused for up to eight years if the home has not changed.

Do I owe my tenant money if I sell my Portland rental?

Possibly. Ending a tenancy without cause or not renewing a fixed term in Portland generally triggers relocation assistance of $2,900 to $4,500 depending on unit size, with 90 days written notice. Some exemptions exist and most require a filing with the Portland Housing Bureau.

How much time does a buyer have to back out after the Oregon disclosure form?

A buyer has five days from delivery of the seller's disclosure statement to revoke, unless the buyer waives that right. If a seller refuses to provide the form, the buyer can revoke an offer at any time before closing.

Can I sell a Portland house with earthquake or landslide concerns?

Yes. Portland sits near the Portland Hills and East Bank faults, and a 2014 report flagged more than 7,000 high-risk locations. You answer the seismic questions on the disclosure form honestly, and a cash buyer will price the house as it stands.

Where is Salem, and how is the city laid out?

Salem is Oregon's capital and the seat of Marion County, in the north-central Willamette Valley. The city covers about 49.6 square miles. The Willamette River runs north through the city and forms the boundary between Marion and Polk counties, so West Salem is in Polk County while the rest of the city is mostly in Marion.

That county line matters to a seller. A house in West Salem and one east of the river can have different county offices, tax collectors and recording steps even though both carry a Salem address.

The 2020 census counted 175,535 residents, which makes Salem the second most populous city in Oregon. Hills frame the city: Salem Hills to the south, Eola Hills to the west at about 1,000 feet, and Waldo Hills to the east at about 600 feet. Elevation inside the city limits ranges from roughly 120 to 800 feet, so some lots are flat valley floor and others sit on slopes.

Salem has 17 recognized neighborhood associations, which are independent groups supported administratively by the city.

What is the history of Salem as a state capital?

Salem grew from the Jason Lee Methodist mission of 1840 and became the territorial capital in 1851 and the state capital when Oregon joined the Union in 1859. The Kalapuya people lived in the area first and called it Chim-i-ki-ti.

The Oregon Institute, forerunner of Willamette University, was set up in 1842, and the town site was established in 1844. The city incorporated in 1857, and the Oregon State Fair was placed here permanently in 1861.

The state capitol burned twice. The first state house was lost in December 1855, and the second capitol, completed in 1876, burned on April 25, 1935. The current building was finished in 1938. Salem's nickname is the Cherry City, from its past cherry-growing industry.

Who are the largest employers in Salem?

State government is Salem's dominant employer, with about 23,500 state employees, which is 26.69 percent of the jobs counted in the city's 2024 financial report. The other large employers are health care, schools, local government and logistics.

Salem is also a food-processing center, with Kettle Foods employing about 700 locally and Oregon Fruit Products canning here since 1935. The Oregon Department of Corrections is headquartered in the city. Median household income was $72,827 in the 2023 American Community Survey.

Public-sector and health-care payrolls make up much of that list, so the local job base looks different from a port or tech-driven city.

What is the weather in Salem, and does it flood?

Salem has a Mediterranean climate with wet winters and dry summers, and yes, parts of the city have a documented flood history. Average annual precipitation is 40.08 inches, most of it from October through April, and July and August together bring only about 2 percent.

The record high is 117 degrees and the record low is minus 12. Flooding is a bigger sales issue than heat.

  • 1861: the largest Willamette flood on record
  • 1964: the Christmas flood crested nearly ten feet above flood stage, caused $157 million in damage and killed 20 Oregonians, and Salem Memorial Hospital evacuated 121 patients
  • February 1996: near 100-year flood levels, and Salem accounted for nearly one-third of Marion County's National Flood Insurance Program claims that year
  • January 2012: more than nine inches of rain in five days in south Salem, flooding in the Battle Creek, Mill Creek, Pringle Creek and Croisan Creek basins, about 300 evacuated and 64 streets closed

The city can tell you whether a parcel is in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area or the floodway, and it keeps a flood insurance rate map and an interactive floodplain map. Development Services answers questions at 503-584-4646. If your house sits near a creek, ask for that determination before you set a closing date. See the city's flood history page.

How do people get around Salem?

Interstate 5 runs through Salem, with Oregon Routes 99E, 22, 221, 51 and 213 also serving the city. Route 22 crosses the river into West Salem on the Marion Street and Center Street bridges.

Cherriots runs the local bus network, including regional service to Wilsonville, and Amtrak stops at the Salem station on the Coast Starlight and Amtrak Cascades routes. McNary Field has limited commercial service, and Avelo Airlines started flights to Burbank and Las Vegas in October 2023.

Salem's main drinking water comes from the North Santiam River watershed rather than the Willamette. Other streams in town include Mill Creek, Mill Race, Pringle Creek and Shelton Ditch, and Riverfront Park links to Minto-Brown Island Park by the Peter Courtney bridge, finished in 2018.

The Salem-Keizer School District, with about 39,000 students, is the second largest in Oregon. A small part of Salem in Marion County falls in Cascade School District 5. Willamette University, Corban University and Chemeketa Community College are all in the area, and Willamette is the oldest university in the American West.

When are Marion County property taxes due on a Salem house?

Marion County property taxes are due November 15, February 15 and May 15, and a full payment by November 15 earns a 3 percent discount. Paying two-thirds by that date earns 2 percent on the amount paid, and paying one-third earns none.

Payments postmarked after the due date lose the discounts and are charged interest. When the 15th falls on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day. For West Salem in Polk County, check with the Polk County tax office instead.

  • By mail: Marion County Tax Collection, PO Box 3416, Portland, OR 97208-3416
  • Online or phone: Paystation, as listed on the county's payment page
  • In person: Courthouse Square, 555 Court Street NE, with after-hours drop boxes
  • Phone: 503-588-5215

Oregon caps growth in assessed value at about 3 percent a year under Measure 50, so a house owned since the 1990s often has an assessed value far below market. The county payment page has the details.

What must a Salem seller disclose?

Oregon sellers deliver a property disclosure statement to each buyer who makes a written offer, and the buyer has five days after delivery to revoke. The form asks about title, water, sewage, structure, systems, seismic issues and general conditions.

Under ORS 105.470, a sale by a court-appointed personal representative, trustee, conservator or guardian, or by a financial institution after foreclosure, can use a shortened Section 1 form.

Floodplain status, creek drainage and any past water damage are the questions most worth answering carefully on a Salem house.

Is Salem in one county?

No. Salem is the seat of Marion County, and the river is the line with Polk County. West Salem lies in Polk County, so tax and recording offices can differ across the river.

When are Marion County property taxes due?

November 15, February 15 and May 15. A full payment by November 15 earns a 3 percent discount, and two-thirds earns 2 percent. If the date lands on a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies.

Has Salem had serious flooding?

Yes. The Willamette flooded in 1861, the Christmas flood of 1964 crested nearly ten feet above flood stage, and January 2012 rains flooded several south Salem creek basins and closed 64 streets.

Who is the largest employer in Salem?

The State of Oregon, with about 23,500 employees. Salem Hospital comes next with 5,829, then the Salem-Keizer School District with 3,499.

Can I sell a Salem house with water damage?

Yes. You disclose what you know on the Oregon seller's form, and a cash buyer prices the house as it stands. Floodplain status can be checked with the city's Development Services office.

Where is Eugene, Oregon, and how is the city laid out?

Eugene is the county seat of Lane County, at the southern end of the Willamette Valley, close to where the McKenzie and Willamette rivers meet. It sits about 110 miles south of Portland and about 50 miles east of the Oregon coast.

The city is divided into 23 neighborhoods, from Whiteaker, Downtown and the two University districts near campus to River Road, Santa Clara, Cal Young, Churchill, Bethel, Far West and the Southwest Hills. Skinner Butte, Spencer Butte and Mount Pisgah give the area its hills, and Amazon Creek runs through town. A hillside lot near Spencer Butte and a house on flat ground in a neighborhood such as Trainsong or Harlow present different repair and access questions.

What is the history of Eugene?

Eugene Skinner built the first pioneer cabin on Skinner's Butte in 1846, and the settlement was named Eugene City in 1853. The cabin became a trading post and an official post office on January 8, 1850.

The town incorporated on October 17, 1862 and dropped the word City in 1889. The University of Oregon was created by the Legislature in 1872 and enrolled its first students on October 16, 1876. Eugene adopted a council and manager form of government in 1944.

Who are the biggest employers in Eugene?

Wood products and recreational vehicle manufacturing are the largest industries, and Bi-Mart and Market of Choice are headquartered here. Lane County reports tourism spending of $1.1 billion in 2023. A job change can push an owner to sell on a short timeline.

How does Eugene's climate affect a house?

Eugene is wet in winter and mild overall, with 40.83 inches of precipitation in an average year and about 7.1 inches of snow. The average annual temperature is 53.1 degrees Fahrenheit.

Moisture is the main wear factor for a Eugene home: roofs, gutters, crawl spaces, siding and decks all take a beating from the long damp season. The weather can also swing the other way. Eugene hit 111 degrees on June 27, 2021, and the record low is minus 12 degrees from December 8, 1972.

Wildfire is a regional concern. The 2020 Holiday Farm Fire burned 173,393 acres in the McKenzie River valley in Lane County between September 7 and October 29, 2020, and many people evacuated to nearby Springfield.

Which school districts serve Eugene?

Eugene School District 4J covers about 85% of the city limits and runs four full-service high schools: Churchill, North Eugene, Sheldon and South Eugene. Bethel School District serves the northwest edge of the city and includes 11 schools.

Higher education includes the University of Oregon, Bushnell University, Lane Community College and a Pacific University campus. Students and faculty create a rental market near campus, and a house's district boundary is one of the first things a buyer's agent checks.

How do roads and transit shape Eugene housing?

Interstate 5 forms much of Eugene's eastern edge, and Oregon Route 99 is the main surface artery through town. Eugene Airport (Mahlon Sweet Field) is the second-largest airport in Oregon.

  • The EmX bus rapid transit line links Eugene and Springfield.
  • The restored 1908 depot downtown is the southern end of two daily Amtrak Cascades trips.

Houses along the EmX corridor and near downtown appeal to people without a car, while hillside and far west properties depend more on driving.

What utilities serve a Eugene house?

The Eugene Water & Electric Board provides both electricity and water to more than 86,000 customers in and around Eugene. It was founded in 1911, is chartered by the city and is governed by an elected five-member board. A seller can ask EWEB about closing or transferring service before the sale date.

What rules apply if I own a rental house in Eugene?

Rental units in Eugene, including rooms for rent, must be registered with the city's Rental Housing Program, and owners must name an emergency contact who lives within 75 miles. The code applies only inside city limits, even if a property has a Eugene mailing address.

  • Rent increases above the state maximum require at least 90 days' notice and relocation assistance equal to two months of rent.
  • Tenants must give written notice before filing a complaint, and the owner then has 10 days to fix a problem (48 hours for essential services).
  • Owners must notify the program when they sell a unit.

An owner who inherits or tires of managing a rental should sort out registration, any open complaints and the tenant's move-out timing before setting a closing date. Details come from the city's Landlord Handbook.

When are property taxes due in Lane County?

Oregon tax statements are mailed by October 25, and you can pay all at once or in three equal parts due November 15, February 15 and May 15. Paying the full amount by November 15 earns a 3% discount, and paying two-thirds by then earns 2%.

Late installments accrue interest at 1.333% per month. If a due date falls on a weekend or holiday it moves to the next business day. Measure 50, approved by voters in 1997, replaced the earlier Measure 47 and applies the 3% limit to assessed value. Lane County collects the tax for Eugene, and a seller should confirm the payoff status with the title company before closing.

What must an Oregon seller disclose?

Under ORS 105.464, a seller of covered residential property must give the buyer a written disclosure statement once the buyer makes a written offer. The form asks about title and boundaries, water and sewage, structure, systems, seismic issues, flooding, settling and other known defects.

A buyer has five days after getting the form to revoke the offer unless they waived that right. Exclusions exist, for example for sales by a court-appointed personal representative or by a bank after foreclosure. The form relies on the seller's actual knowledge, so answer honestly, and note that it contains no "as is" language.

What do sellers in Eugene usually face?

  • Older homes with deferred roof, moisture or sewer-line work after years of wet winters.
  • Inherited houses where several family members must agree and probate or a trust must be settled first.
  • Rental houses with tenants, registration paperwork and relocation rules to follow.
  • A student-driven calendar near the university, where timing around the school year changes how fast a house moves.
  • Owners behind on payments who want a certain closing date.

When condition or timing is the problem, many Eugene owners compare a traditional listing against a direct cash sale. A cash buyer purchases the house in its current state, so repairs, showings and buyer financing drop out of the picture. Does Eugene have a transfer tax on home sales?

The county transfer tax in Washington County is set by that county's own code, Chapter 3.04. We could not confirm from an official page whether Lane County has any similar charge, so ask the title or escrow company to confirm what applies to a Eugene sale. Title, escrow and recording charges still apply and are set by the companies and the county clerk.

The Census Bureau counted 176,654 residents in the 2020 Census, and the Bureau's estimate for July 1, 2025 is 178,618.

Do I need to register a rental house before selling it in Eugene?

Yes, if it is a rental inside city limits, it should be registered with the Rental Housing Program, and the program expects to be told when a unit is sold. Ask the city if you are unsure of a unit's status.

How long do Eugene property tax installments run?

Oregon bills in three parts due November 15, February 15 and May 15, with a 3% discount for paying in full by November 15. Interest of 1.333% per month applies after each due date.

Can I sell a Eugene house with tenants living in it?

Yes, the sale is possible, but the tenant's lease and Oregon and Eugene notice rules continue to apply. Talk to a landlord-tenant attorney if move-out timing is part of the plan.

Where is Gresham, Oregon?

Gresham has 16 recognized neighborhoods: Central City, Centennial, Gresham Butte, Historic Southeast, Hogan Cedars, Hollybrook, Kelly Creek, North Central, North Gresham, Northeast, Northwest, Pleasant Valley, Powell Valley, Rockwood, Southwest and Wilkes East.

The city's trail network includes the Springwater Corridor, the 40-Mile Loop and the Gresham-Fairview Trail, and Main City Park sits near downtown.

What does the Gresham economy look like?

Gresham is described as the economic center for eastern Multnomah County, and it grew from a farming town into a city of more than 100,000. Mount Hood Medical Center, which opened as Gresham General Hospital in 1959, and the community college are anchors in town.

Countywide, major industries include manufacturing, transportation, wholesale and retail trade and tourism, and the Port of Portland is a significant West Coast shipping hub. About 27% of Gresham residents hold a bachelor's degree, according to Census figures cited by Wikipedia.

Which school districts serve Gresham?

Three districts serve the city: Centennial, Gresham-Barlow and Reynolds. High schools include Gresham, Sam Barlow, Springwater Trail, Centennial and Reynolds, and Mount Hood Community College is in Gresham.

Because the city is split among three districts, the address matters. Two houses a few blocks apart can feed different schools, and sellers should be ready to tell buyers which district a property belongs to.

How do I get around Gresham?

  • Interstate 84 provides western access, and U.S. Route 26 provides eastern access.
  • TriMet buses and the MAX Blue Line light rail serve the city, with the Blue Line's eastern end at Cleveland Avenue.
  • The fareless Sandy Area Metro shuttle connects Gresham to Sandy.

Gresham sits at the eastern end of the Portland metro transit network, which matters to commuters weighing a house here against one closer in.

What does Gresham's weather mean for a house?

Gresham has a Mediterranean climate with wet winters and dry summers, and December is the wettest month at 7.61 inches of rain. The mean daily high is 82 degrees in July and August and 46 degrees in January, and the average low in January is 35 degrees.

That much winter rain keeps pressure on roofs, gutters, siding and crawl spaces. Snow is light at 5.8 inches a year, with relative humidity averaging 75%.

How is Gresham governed, and what landmarks does it have?

Gresham uses a council and manager form of government, with a mayor and six councilors who serve four-year terms. The city manager, Eric Schmidt, was appointed in June 2024.

Historic sites include the Gresham Carnegie Library, built in 1913, and the Jacob Zimmerman House, built in 1874, both on the National Register of Historic Places. Gresham Pioneer Cemetery was founded in 1859. Mount Hood Community College, in Gresham, offers associate degrees and bachelor's programs through a partnership with Eastern Oregon University.

Can I add or rent out an accessory dwelling unit in Gresham?

Gresham allows accessory dwelling units, which the city caps by size, and renting one requires a residential rental license. Short-term rentals, including bed and breakfasts, are prohibited in an ADU.

  • Conversions or ADUs attached to the house: up to 900 square feet.
  • ADUs beside or behind a garage: up to 750 square feet, including the garage.
  • Freestanding ADUs: 750 square feet or 50% of the house size, whichever is less.
  • Three paved on-site parking spaces, each 8.5 feet by 18 feet.

Simple conversions go through Type I review in about two to three weeks, while attached additions that enlarge the footprint and most freestanding units go through Type II review that takes roughly three to four months. An existing ADU without permits can complicate a sale, so confirm its status with the city planner.

When are Multnomah County property taxes due?

Oregon statements go out by October 25, and the three installments are due November 15, February 15 and May 15. Pay in full by November 15 to save 3%, or pay two-thirds to save 2%.

Interest on a late installment runs at 1.333% per month, starting December 16, February 16 or May 16. Taxes under $40 cannot be split. Oregon Measure 50 was approved on May 20, 1997, and replaced Measure 47. Ask the title company for the current payoff and any unpaid installments before closing.

What must a Gresham seller tell the buyer?

Oregon sellers of covered residential property must give each buyer who submits a written offer a signed disclosure statement under ORS 105.464. It asks about title, water, sewage, structure, systems, flooding, settling and other defects, and the buyer has five days to revoke the offer unless they waived that right.

Exclusions include a sale by a personal representative, trustee or conservator and a bank sale after foreclosure. The form relies on what the seller actually knows, so list problems you are aware of instead of leaving them blank.

What do Gresham sellers usually face?

  • Houses from the suburban building boom that need roof, window or drainage updates.
  • Inherited homes in neighborhoods such as Rockwood or Historic Southeast, where heirs live elsewhere.
  • Landlords with tenants in a house they no longer want to manage.
  • Owners with unpermitted ADUs or garage conversions.
  • Homeowners behind on payments who want certainty on timing.

A cash sale lets an owner skip repairs and showings. We buy houses in Gresham in their current condition, and the offer request takes only a few minutes.

More questions about Gresham, OR

How many people live in Gresham?

The Census Bureau counted 114,247 residents in 2020, and its July 1, 2025 estimate is 111,513. Gresham is the fourth largest city in Oregon.

Does Multnomah County charge a transfer tax on home sales?

Washington County sets its own transfer tax under its county code, Chapter 3.04. We could not confirm an official Multnomah County transfer tax, so ask the title or escrow company what applies to a Gresham sale. Closing costs for title and escrow still apply.

When is the first Oregon property tax installment due?

November 15. The other two are due February 15 and May 15, and a 3% discount applies to full payment by November 15.

Can a Gresham house be sold if it has an unpermitted ADU?

It can be sold, but the buyer may ask about permits and the city treats ADUs under specific size, parking and review rules. Speak with the city's Planner on Duty if the status is unclear.

Which school district is my Gresham house in?

It depends on the address. Gresham is served by the Centennial, Gresham-Barlow and Reynolds districts, so check the district's boundary map for the exact property.

Where is Bend, Oregon, and what is the terrain like?

Bend is a Central Oregon city on the Deschutes River, east of the Cascade Range, and it is the county seat of Deschutes County. It covers about 35 square miles at an elevation near 3,640 feet.

Pilot Butte, an extinct cinder cone, stands inside city limits. The Horse Lava Tube System borders the east side, Newberry National Volcanic Monument lies just south, and Deschutes National Forest touches the southwest edge. Across Deschutes County the U.S. Forest Service owns about 51 percent of the land.

Bend's 2020 census population was 99,178, up 29.4 percent from 76,639 in 2010. The Wikipedia summary of Census Bureau data gives an estimate of 106,926 for 2024.

How did Bend get started?

Bend takes its name from a bend in the Deschutes River that pioneers forded, and it was platted in 1904 and incorporated in January 1905. A dam built in 1910 created Mirror Pond, and Deschutes County was formed in 1916 with Bend as its seat.

Lumber carried the early economy. When the Shevlin-Hixon Lumber mill closed in 1950, the region took its largest economic drop since the Great Depression. POWDR Corp. bought Mt. Bachelor in 2001.

What are the biggest employers in Bend?

St. Charles Health System is Bend's largest employer, followed by the Bend-La Pine School District. Tourism is also a major sector: Travel Oregon reported in 2019 that the local industry employed about 10,000 people.

Retirement and commuting to tech jobs in the Bay Area and Seattle also drive growth. Visitors matter to the local budget: transient room tax revenue topped $7.8 million from July 2024 to March 2025. Deschutes Brewery is the largest of more than 30 breweries in the city, and four destination resorts, including Sunriver, are major employers in the wider county. That visitor economy is why the short-term rental rules below come up so often.

What is Bend's climate and how does it affect a house?

Bend has a cold semi-arid climate with light precipitation but real winters. The city gets about 10.6 inches of precipitation and 21.6 inches of snow a year. January highs average 42.5 degrees and lows 24.6. July highs average 83.8.

The record low is minus 26, and freezing temperatures are possible from about mid-September to mid-June. Summer days can swing 35 degrees from high to low.

  • Frozen pipes and shallow water lines are a winter risk in vacant houses
  • Roof snow load and ice dams matter for older roofs
  • Dry summers raise wildfire concerns for houses near trees and the national forest
  • Big day and night swings stress paint, decks and exterior wood

A house left empty over winter can develop plumbing damage quickly, and an inherited or second-home property is often vacant.

How does wildfire risk affect selling a Bend house?

Wildfire risk shows up in Bend as insurance cost and availability, not as a statewide map. Oregon's legislature passed Senate Bill 83 in 2025 to repeal the state wildfire hazard map and its building code requirements.

Before the repeal, Deschutes County had 21,258 lots classified as high hazard. A 2023 law already barred insurers from using the map for pricing or coverage. Central Oregon owners still reported large premium increases and coverage cutbacks, and the state notes that insurers use their own models.

The Oregon Division of Financial Regulation lists these defensible space steps:

  • Clear dry leaves, brush and pine needles from the yard and gutters
  • Trim trees back from the structure
  • Screen open vents

If your Bend house has fire-prone landscaping or a rough roof, an as-is sale lets the buyer decide how to handle it. The state's page on wildfire and insurance explains policyholder rights.

Which parts of Bend are there, and what are the schools?

Bend has 13 official neighborhood districts: Awbrey Butte, Boyd Acres, Century West, Larkspur, Mountain View, Old Bend, Old Farm District, Orchard District, River West, Southeast Bend, Southern Crossing, Southwest Bend and Summit West.

The Bend-La Pine School District has six high schools, six middle schools and 19 elementary schools, three of them magnet schools. Central Oregon Community College and OSU-Cascades are also in Bend.

Housing tenure in 2020 was 60.6 percent owner-occupied and 39.4 percent renter-occupied, with 44,449 housing units.

How do roads, buses and airports connect Bend?

US 20 and US 97 meet in Bend, and US 97 runs through the city as the Bend Parkway. Century Drive, Highway 372, leads to Mt. Bachelor.

Roberts Field in Redmond, 18 miles north, has direct flights to cities including Seattle, Denver, Los Angeles and San Francisco. Bend Municipal Airport handles general aviation. The nearest Amtrak station is in Chemult, about 65 miles south. Cascades East Transit runs nine fixed bus routes from the Hawthorne Transit Center.

What are the short-term rental rules if my Bend house is a vacation rental?

Bend requires a land use permit and an operating license for most short-term rentals, and permits approved after April 15, 2015 end when the property sells. A short-term rental is a stay of fewer than 30 consecutive days.

  • Operating licenses are never transferable
  • Permits approved on or before April 15, 2015 run with the land, and the new owner must apply for an operating license within 60 days of closing
  • A City of Bend business registration is required
  • Most rentals owe a 10.4 percent room tax on gross revenue

In practice, a buyer of a vacation rental cannot assume the rental income will carry over. Check with the City's Licensing office, at 541-388-5580 extension 8, and planning at extension 3 before you promote the house as an income property. The city's short-term rental page lists current fees, which the sources I read showed in conflicting amounts.

Can I sell a Bend rental with a tenant in place?

Yes, and with 39.4 percent of Bend housing renter-occupied in 2020, many owners do. Oregon's ORS 90.427 limits ending a tenancy for a sale: after the tenant's first year, a landlord needs an accepted offer from a buyer who will live in the home and must give at least 90 days of written notice.

The landlord also owes one month's rent when delivering that notice, unless the landlord owns four or fewer covered units. A landlord who breaks the rule can owe three months' rent plus damages, so a sale that keeps the lease in place is often the lower-risk route.

How do Deschutes County property taxes work for a Bend seller?

Deschutes County sends Bend property tax statements in October, and the first installment and the full-pay discount fall in mid-November. For the 2025 bills, the deadline was November 17, with a 3 percent discount for paying in full and 2 percent for paying two thirds.

Installment (2025 bills)Date

Central Oregon Daily reported that Deschutes County property taxes were expected to rise about 4 percent in 2025, depending on location. The county's tax office is at 541-388-6540 or taxoffice@deschutes.org, and the county asks owners to update a mailing address before September 30 so the statement reaches the right place.

If you sell mid-year, the escrow company prorates the bill between you and the buyer. Oregon's Department of Revenue lists December 31 as the appeal deadline to the county Board of Property Tax Appeals.

More questions about Bend, OR

Is Bend in Deschutes County?

Yes. Bend is the county seat of Deschutes County, which was formed on December 13, 1916.

Does selling a Bend vacation rental transfer the short-term rental permit?

Not for newer permits. Permits approved after April 15, 2015 are tied to the owner and become void when the property sells, and operating licenses never transfer.

What is Bend's coldest recorded temperature?

The record low is minus 26 degrees, recorded in January and February, according to the Wikipedia climate summary.

When are Bend property taxes due?

For the 2025 bills, the full-pay deadline was November 17, with the later installments due February 17 and May 15. Dates move when November 15 lands on a weekend.

Can I sell a Bend house with wildfire risk or old landscaping?

Yes. Oregon repealed its state wildfire hazard map in 2025, but insurers still price risk with their own models, so buyers should expect questions about defensible space.

Where is Beaverton, Oregon, and what is it next to?

Beaverton is a city in Washington County on the eastern edge of the Tualatin Valley, just west of the Tualatin Mountains. It borders Portland to the east, Hillsboro to the west and Tigard to the south.

The city covers 19.61 square miles. Elevation within city limits runs from about 132 feet to about 698 feet, so some streets sit on noticeable hills. The 2020 census counted 97,494 residents, which makes Beaverton the second-largest city in Washington County and the seventh-largest in Oregon.

The city has 13 neighborhoods, among them Central Beaverton, Denney Whitford, Raleigh West, Five Oaks, Triple Creek, Highland, South Beaverton, Vose and West Slope. Buyers and sellers here usually talk about a house by its neighborhood and its school boundary more than by the city name.

How did Beaverton develop?

Beaverton grew from an 1840s farming settlement into a suburb that was incorporated in 1893. The Atfalati people lived in the area first, and the Hall family filed the first land claim in 1847.

  • 1860: a plank road from Portland was completed
  • 1872: the first post office opened
  • 1893: the city was incorporated with about 400 residents
  • 2020: the population reached 97,494, up 8.6 percent from 89,803 in 2010

The city's urban growth boundary has been expanded, including the Cooper Mountain urban reserve area added in 2018.

Nike is Beaverton's largest employer by a wide margin, followed by the Beaverton School District. The city sits in the Silicon Forest tech corridor and is an economic center for Washington County alongside Hillsboro.

What is the weather like in Beaverton and how does it affect a house?

Beaverton has wet winters and dry summers, with about 39 inches of rain a year, most of it between October and April. December is the wettest month at 6.53 inches.

Snow is minor at about 1.9 inches a year. Heat is the bigger swing: July and August highs run near 80 degrees, and the record high is 115 degrees, set in June. The record low is minus 8.

  • Gutters, downspouts and roof condition matter after a long wet season

A house with a leaking roof or a wet crawl space can stall a financed sale because the lender's appraiser may flag it. Cash purchases avoid that step.

How do MAX, WES and the highways shape Beaverton?

TriMet's MAX light rail has seven stations in the city: Elmonica/SW 170th Avenue, Merlo Road/SW 158th Avenue, Beaverton Creek, Millikan Way, Beaverton Central, Beaverton Transit Center and Sunset Transit Center. The Blue Line serves all seven and the Red Line serves the last two.

Beaverton Transit Center is TriMet's busiest and is the northern end of WES commuter rail, which also stops at Hall/Nimbus. US 26, the Sunset Highway, links the city to Portland, Hillsboro and the coast, and Oregon 217 runs south through Tigard to I-5.

A house within walking distance of a MAX station is a different product from one that needs a car for every errand. Tell any buyer which one you have.

Which school districts serve Beaverton?

Most of Beaverton is in the Beaverton School District, which has six public high schools: Aloha, Beaverton, Mountainside, Southridge, Sunset and Westview. Portions of the city fall in the Hillsboro School District and in Portland Public Schools.

Private options include Jesuit High School, Valley Catholic School and Southwest Christian School. Tualatin Valley Fire and Rescue provides fire protection, and the city's Public Safety Center opened in fall 2020.

Does Beaverton have a real estate transfer tax?

Yes. Washington County charges a transfer tax of $1 per $1,000 of selling price on real property transfers, which Oregon law otherwise generally bars local governments from imposing. State law, ORS 306.815, prohibits most local transfer taxes but carves out taxes that were already in effect on March 31, 1997.

The county's Real Property Transfer Tax Ordinance is Washington County Code Chapter 3.04. At that rate, a $500,000 sale would carry $500 in transfer tax.

The county's exemption form lists many transfers that are not taxed, and a claim must be filed within 15 days of tendering the documents for recording.

  • Transfers by gift, devise or inheritance
  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure and court-ordered transfers in foreclosure or bankruptcy
  • Transfers between spouses under a court order in a divorce
  • Conveyances to or from a government entity
  • Transfers with a selling price of $13,999 or less

Ask your escrow officer who is paying the tax on your particular sale and where it appears on the settlement statement.

What should Beaverton landlords know before selling a rented house?

More than half of Beaverton's occupied homes are rented, so many sellers here are landlords. About 52.5 percent of homes are renter-occupied and 47.5 percent are owner-occupied.

Where is Medford, Oregon, and what is the land like?

Medford is the county seat of Jackson County, in the Rogue Valley about 27 miles north of the California border. It sits at 1,434 feet in a rain shadow between the Cascade Range and the Siskiyou Mountains, which explains the dry summers.

Roxy Ann Peak rises to 3,576 feet at the edge of town, and Prescott Park around it covers 1,740 acres. Bear Creek Park runs nearly 100 acres, and Alba Park, deeded to the city in 1888, is the oldest. Houses on the foothills and houses on the valley floor face different slopes, drainage and fire exposure, so describe the lot as well as the building.

How did Medford get its start?

Medford began as a railroad survey stop. Surveyors working on the Oregon and California Railroad route in 1883 included David Loring, who named the town for Medford, Massachusetts.

  • The town was platted in early December 1883 with 82 blocks.
  • The first post office opened February 6, 1884.
  • Medford incorporated as a town on February 24, 1885, and as a city in 1905.
  • It took the county seat from Jacksonville in 1927.
  • Interstate 5 was completed through town in 1967.

That timeline matters for sellers because it explains the mix of old railroad-era streets near downtown and newer subdivisions farther out.

  • Lithia Motors, a Fortune 500 company, has been headquartered in Medford since 1970.

With seasonal work at Harry and David and shift work in health care, a rental's tenant mix can turn over on a different calendar than a typical house, so check lease end dates before you set a closing date.

How hot and dry does Medford get, and what does that do to a house?

Medford has a Mediterranean climate with hot summers and dry air. Summers average 61 afternoons above 90 degrees and 11 above 100, and the record high is 115 degrees, reached July 20, 1946 and again June 28, 2021.

Annual precipitation averages 18.43 inches and snowfall 3.4 inches. Winter temperature inversions can hold fog in the valley for weeks. Long hot spells age roofing, exterior paint and air conditioning equipment, and a buyer's inspector will look at all three.

How did the Almeda fire affect Medford housing?

The Almeda fire started the morning of September 8, 2020, and swept through the Rogue Valley within hours. Jefferson Public Radio reported more than 2,600 homes destroyed between Ashland, Talent, Phoenix and Medford, calling it the most destructive wildfire in Oregon's recorded history.

Medford lost homes too, including a mobile home park in the city. A year later, thousands of displaced residents had not received the federal help they needed to rebuild. For a seller, the effects show up in two ways:

  • Fire-damaged or rebuilt properties may carry insurance, permit or valuation questions that a buyer will ask about.
  • Under ORS 308.146, a fire or other act of God that cuts a property's real market value also reduces its maximum assessed value for that year.

Oregon lawmakers passed a bill in 2025 to repeal the state's contested wildfire hazard map, which the statewide defensible space and building code requirements relied on. Joseph Avery built the first home within today's city limits in 1845 or 1846 and platted a supply town called Marysville in 1849. The Territorial Legislature renamed it Corvallis in 1853, and the city was incorporated on January 29, 1857.

A faction briefly made Corvallis the territorial capital in 1855 before the capital returned to Salem. Land donated in 1851 for the county seat is where the Benton County Courthouse stands today.

During the first year, a month-to-month tenancy can end without cause on 30 days' notice. Violations can cost three months' rent plus damages, and the tenant has up to a year to bring the claim.

The Corvallis School District runs two high schools, Corvallis High School and Crescent Valley High School, and both draw students from parts of the city. Linn-Benton Community College has a Benton Center campus here.

Oregon 34 links Corvallis to I-5 and to Philomath, US 20 leads to Albany, and Oregon 99W runs to Eugene and McMinnville. Corvallis Transit System runs nine routes and has been fareless since 2011.

Biking is unusually common. A 2009 figure put bicycle commuting at 9.3 percent, the highest of any U.S. metro area, and a 2013 count had 72.6 percent driving alone and 7.7 percent working from home. Benton County is small, covering 679 square miles, which makes it the fourth-smallest Oregon county by land area. It borders Polk County to the north, Lincoln County to the west, Linn County to the east and Lane County to the south.

Besides Corvallis, the county includes Adair Village, Monroe, Philomath and the part of Albany north of downtown. Its 2025 population estimate is 97,728, so Corvallis holds well over half of the county's residents.

Springfield began as farmland settled in the late 1840s and took its name from a natural spring in a prairie. The Kalapuya people had lived in the valley first and used controlled burning to keep it open.

William Stevens claimed land in October 1847, and Elias and Mary Briggs arrived in 1848. Springfield School District No. 19 was formed in 1854, and the city incorporated on February 25, 1885.

Where is Albany, Oregon, and how is the city laid out?

What is Albany's history in brief?

Albany was settled in the 1840s, named a county seat in 1851 and incorporated as a city in 1864. The Kalapuya people lived here first, and treaties and disease displaced them in the 1850s.

The railroad arrived in 1871 and the Santiam Canal was finished in 1872. The Albany Research Center opened in 1942 and helped start the local rare metals industry. The October 1962 Columbus Day Storm hit the area hard.

Linn County itself is known for grass seed, and local farms also grow corn, beans, mint, strawberries and hazelnuts. Because jobs are spread across factories, a hospital and a community college, house demand does not hang on one company.

Since 1985, designated buildings in the districts and those on the landmark inventory have gone through review for exterior alterations, additions and demolition. Planning staff or the Landmarks Commission handles it. The city favors repair over replacement and asks for matching materials when replacement is unavoidable. That review applies to whoever owns the house next. Sellers with a worn porch or failing siding in Monteith or Hackleman often face a repair list that a buyer has to carry out under those rules. Selling as-is moves that job to the buyer.

Amtrak's Coast Starlight and Amtrak Cascades stop at the Albany station on 10th Avenue SW. Local buses include Albany Transit System, the Linn-Benton Loop and the Valley Retriever, with the last two linking to Corvallis. The nearest commercial airports are Eugene to the south and Portland to the north.

Where is Grants Pass, Oregon?

Grants Pass is the county seat of Josephine County, on Interstate 5 along the Rogue River in southern Oregon's Rogue Valley, northwest of Medford. The city sits at about 960 feet of elevation and covers roughly 11 square miles.

Josephine County itself is large, at 1,642 square miles and 88,090 residents in the 2020 Census. Most of the land belongs to the federal government: the Forest Service owns about 39% and the Bureau of Land Management about 28%. How did Grants Pass get its name and start?

The city says its name honors Ulysses S. Grant's success in the Vicksburg Campaign. Fur trappers passed through from the 1820s along the Siskiyou Trail, and settlers on the Applegate Trail came through in the late 1840s.

The post office opened on March 22, 1865, and the city incorporated in 1887. Voters moved the county seat here from Kerby in an 1886 vote. The Caveman Bridge on 6th Street, designed by Conde McCullough, dates from 1933 and was refurbished in 2019.

A sugar beet factory opened in 1916, but its processing machinery moved to Toppenish, Washington around 1918 and 1919. The Rogue River itself remains the city's defining feature, and the area's hot-summer Mediterranean climate fits USDA hardiness zone 8b. In City of Grants Pass v. Johnson, decided June 28, 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that cities may enforce public camping bans even without enough shelter space. The case was brought against the City of Grants Pass.

Late payments accrue interest at 1.333% per month. Josephine County has had budget strain: voters rejected a $12 million levy in November 2014, which led to 70 layoffs and the release of about 90 jail inmates.

Where is Redmond, Oregon, and what kind of place is it?

Redmond is a city in Deschutes County, on the eastern side of the Cascade Range in Oregon's High Desert. It sits at about 3,012 feet, roughly 17 miles north of Bend, which is the county seat. Portland is 146 miles away, Salem 129 miles and Eugene 126 miles.

The city is compact, at about 18.6 square miles, and almost all of it is land. The Horse Lava Tube System runs into the city at the Redmond Caves, a reminder that the ground under many lots here is volcanic rock.

The Census Bureau puts Redmond at 38,547 residents as of July 1, 2025. That is up from 33,274 in the 2020 census and 26,215 in 2010.

How did Redmond grow into the city it is today?

Redmond was founded in 1904, platted in 1906 and incorporated on July 6, 1910, and it took its name from Frank T. Redmond, who settled the area in 1905. An irrigation canal built by the company that became part of the Central Oregon Irrigation District made farming and town building possible.

The Oregon Trunk Railway and electric service both arrived in 1911. During the 1940s the city was home to a U.S. Army air base, and commercial flights started at Roberts Field after World War II. The population then sat nearly flat from the 1950s through most of the 1980s.

Redmond has a dry steppe climate with sunny days and cool nights, and the main wear on a house comes from sun, temperature swings and winter freezes. Annual precipitation is only about 8 to 10 inches, which is far drier than the Willamette Valley.

Summer daytime highs usually run from 75 to 100 degrees, and winter highs often sit between 10 and 40. The growing season is short, since in half of the years from 1971 to 2000 the last freeze came after July 3.

  • Wood decks and fences dry out and crack over the years.

Fire access has come up locally. At a May 2025 city council hearing on a new subdivision, a nearby resident raised the point that the area had only one good way out in a fire. That resident pointed to the neighborhood's closeness to the urban growth boundary.

Redmond's economy centers on aviation, manufacturing, distribution and tourism around the airport and the surrounding resorts. The city's economic development group, REDI, lists nine target industries.

  • Bioscience and medical devices
  • Brewing and distilling

The Redmond Air Center at the airport is a U.S. Forest Service base for smokejumpers, firefighting and training, and Oregon's only smokejumper base since 1981. Eagle Crest Resort, about 6 miles west of town, is one of eight destination resorts in the state and one of the county's largest corporate taxpayers. REDI also reports a four-year university and a community college in the area, and George Fox University runs a secondary campus in Redmond.

How does Roberts Field affect Redmond house sales?

Roberts Field is Redmond's city-run airport and the only commercial passenger airport in Central Oregon, and it also serves Bend. Alaska, American, Delta and United fly there, and it is the third-busiest commercial airport in Oregon after Portland and Eugene. Passenger traffic reached 1,317,665 in 2025.

A $180 million expansion began in 2025 with federal help. For sellers, the airport is a source of jobs and of out-of-town buyers,, and homes near the flight paths may hear aircraft.

Other transport links are simple. U.S. Route 97 runs north and south through the city on the Redmond Parkway alignment that opened in 2008, Oregon Route 126 meets it and heads west toward Eugene and east to Prineville, and a BNSF main line crosses town. The nearest Amtrak stop is Chemult, about 75 miles south.

Is Redmond adding new houses, and how does that change a sale?

Yes. The Redmond City Council approves new subdivisions under its Redmond 2050 Comprehensive Plan, and recent approvals include a 32-home subdivision called Antelope Flats in southwest Redmond. Groundbreaking was expected six months to a year after approval, with about two years of construction after that.

New supply near your neighborhood can compete with a resale house for the same buyers. It can also bring new streets, utilities and traffic. Staff noted that access on southwest Antelope Avenue did not yet meet partial roadway standards, so road work is part of some projects.

If your house is near open land, check the city's planning pages for pending applications before you set a timeline.

How do Deschutes County property taxes work for a Redmond home?

Deschutes County collects tax on Redmond homes, with payments due November 16, February 16 and May 17 for the 2026-2027 year. Paying in full by November 16 earns a 3 percent discount and paying two-thirds earns 2 percent, while installment payments get no discount. Interest starts to accrue on December 16.

Statements were expected online by October 20 and in the mail by October 25. Mailed payments must be postmarked by the due date, and metered postmarks from mail machines are not accepted. The property tax office is at 1300 NW Wall Street, Suite 203, in Bend, and the phone number is 541-388-6540. There is a drop box in Redmond with limited hours.

Oregon assessed values generally cannot rise more than about 3 percent a year under Measure 50, so a Redmond house owned for many years may carry a low assessed value. Tax proration between buyer and seller is handled through the escrow company at closing. See the Deschutes County payment page for current details.

An Oregon seller gives each buyer who makes a written offer a property disclosure statement, and the buyer has five days after delivery to revoke unless that right is waived. The form covers title, water, sewage, structure, systems and general conditions.

It is a hub for jobs and travel. Roberts Field has commercial service from four airlines, and the Redmond Air Center there is a U.S. Forest Service smokejumper and firefighting base.

It can. Residents have raised fire access at a city council hearing, and buyers may ask the same questions. Answer the disclosure form questions honestly and ask your insurer what it needs.

Yes. An as-is sale is allowed in Oregon, though you still give the buyer the disclosure statement unless an exclusion applies. A cash buyer prices the house in its present condition.

A water-powered elevator linked the two tiers in 1915, was converted to electricity in the 1920s and replaced by a new electric elevator in 1952. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. If your house is on the bluff, say so, since buyers care about slope, views and walking access.

Which Oregon City neighborhoods come up most?

The city lists 12 official neighborhood associations. Three areas stand out in descriptions of the city.

  • McLoughlin sits on the bluff above downtown and has many older homes, the McLoughlin House, the public library, a pool and a hospital.

Oregon City was the end of the Oregon Trail and the first U.S. city west of the Rocky Mountains to incorporate. Dr. John McLoughlin of the Hudson's Bay Company founded the settlement in 1829 to use Willamette Falls to power a lumber mill, and the city incorporated in 1844.

If your house is in a designated historic area, exterior changes need city review before work starts. Oregon City's list includes the Canemah National Register District and the McLoughlin Conservation District, which spans streets from 1st through 12th.

Planning staff can say whether a property is designated at ocplanning@orcity.org or 503-722-3789. A buyer who plans changes will ask, so find out before you list.

How did Forest Grove begin?

The Atfalati band of the Kalapuya people lived on the Tualatin Plains before Euro-American settlement. Alvin T. and Abigail Smith settled in 1841, and Smith became the first postmaster on February 1, 1850, with his log cabin serving as the post office.

Trustees of Tualatin Academy, later Pacific University, chose the name on January 10, 1851, after a grove of oak trees on the campus. Forest Grove incorporated in 1872, the first city in Washington County. Rail service arrived with the Oregon Electric in November 1908 and the Southern Pacific in January 1914. Red Electric passenger service ended in 1929 and the Oregon Electric stopped running in 1932.

The city counted 547 people in 1880, 1,772 in 1910, 17,708 in 2000 and 21,083 in 2010. The 2020 Census count of 26,225 means about 5,000 more residents in ten years, and 99.7% of residents live in urban areas. Sales by court-appointed personal representatives and trustees are excluded from Oregon's seller disclosure rules under ORS 105.470. So are sales by a financial institution that took the property through foreclosure.

Other sellers of one-to-four-unit homes must provide a signed disclosure statement to each buyer who makes a written offer. If a buyer gets one, they have five business days to revoke unless they signed a waiver. Getting the right paperwork lined up first keeps an inherited sale from stalling.

How does Newberg fit into Yamhill County?

Newberg shares Yamhill County with McMinnville, Lafayette and Sheridan. The county covers 718 square miles, counted 107,722 residents in 2020, and is the fifth-smallest county in Oregon by area.

Wine is a large part of the county economy. Yamhill has more vineyard acreage than any other Oregon county, with over 80 wineries and six American Viticultural Areas wholly or partly inside its borders. Logging remains the mainstay of the western part of the county. A Newberg seller with acreage or a rural lot should ask which tax and land-use rules apply before pricing it.

  • Listing with an agent versus accepting an as-is offer from a cash buyer.

  • Whether a tenant or a college renter is in the house.
  • Whether the lot is inside city limits, since city and county rules differ for rural parcels in Yamhill County.

Each buyer sets its own terms, so ask for them in writing before you decide.
